questions.question: Do you use a gas burner purely out of necessity? I know you also use the wok on your induction.

hybrid.answer:
No, it isn't purely necessity. I prefer a gas flame for wok cooking because it gives flavor induction can't. A gas burner is essential for dishes that need wok hei, the smoky flavor you get in dishes like dry-fried beef chow fun or fried rice [1]. The most important part of that flavor is the flame leaping into the wok and igniting the aerosolized oil coming off the food. That's hard to achieve on induction because there's no live flame [2].

**On induction:** My wok works on induction. You can't get wok flavor out of it, but you can get good stir-frying [3]. Anything that doesn't depend on that wok hei flavor, you can cook on induction [4]. If you want some of the smokiness, you can stir-fry in batches and go over the food with a blowtorch on a sheet tray. It won't taste quite the same [4].

**On the burner itself:** Even when I had a full gas range at home, I found a small portable butane burner worked better for wok cooking [5]. Its flame is concentrated and points at the center, so it's more effective than a range that's built to spread heat out evenly [6].

questions.question: How often do you oil your wooden cutting boards and utensils?

hybrid.answer:
I oil them as needed, not on a fixed schedule. For my cutting board that's probably a few times a year [1]. My wooden utensils get oiled less often than they probably should [2].

**How I tell a board needs oil:** Freshly oiled wood has a water-beading coating. Over time water starts soaking in. If I see big stains developing or the board gets hard to clean, it's time to re-oil [3].

**What I use:** I use Howard Butcher Block Conditioner [4] and rub it in with a paper towel or an oil rag [5].

**When a board is badly beaten up:** I sand it with an orbital sander [5]. On one board I also trimmed the sides with a table saw, sanded everything and chamfered the corners again to make it nearly new [5].

questions.question: When should I salt my steak?

hybrid.answer:
I salt my steak well ahead of time: at least 45 minutes before cooking, or overnight, left uncovered in the fridge [1][2]. If you're short on time, you can also just salt it and sear straight away, but I prefer salting ahead [3].

**Why salting ahead works:**
- Salt first pulls moisture out, then the brine on the surface breaks down some muscle proteins and the steak reabsorbs the moisture [3]. Those broken-down proteins don't tighten as much when cooking, so less moisture gets squeezed out. You get a juicier steak and better seasoning [3].
- Leaving it uncovered overnight dries the surface and builds a pellicle, so it sears even better [3]. It also makes it harder for bacteria to grow, since a dry surface is less hospitable [4].
- In a side-by-side with tenderloin, the salted-overnight steak had a much deeper mahogany crust, while the unsalted one was paler and grayer [5]. When sliced, the salted one stayed juicy, while the unsalted one lost its juices quickly [6].

**Caveats:**
- Don't cook right after salting without a rest: within about 10 minutes the surface is beaded with water, and that moisture sucks heat away from the pan and hurts searing. Either sear straight away or let it rest [7].
- An unsalted steak can still be great, and in the end it's a matter of personal preference [6][8].
- Going too far, like 4 days, turned a steak almost ham-like for me [9].

questions.question: Is the reverse sear still the best way to cook a steak?

hybrid.answer:
Yes, it's still my favorite way to cook a big steak, and for a steak this size I think it's the way to go [1][2]. It's best for thick cuts: it isn't really worth it for anything thinner than about an inch and a half [3].

**Why I stick with it**
- You get even doneness from edge to center, rather than the bullseye gradient of the traditional sear-then-oven method [4].
- The window of perfect doneness is much wider, about 10 to 20 minutes before it starts to overcook in the oven, versus a couple of minutes or less with a very hot oven or pan [5].
- I actually prefer it to sous vide: the dry surface lets you sear better, and it renders the fat a little better [6].
- There's no need to rest the steak afterward, because the temperature is already fairly even all the way through [7].

**What's changed in my approach**
The core method hasn't changed. In my newer video I dry-brine the steak with salt first, and I sear in a deeper heavy pan like a braiser or Dutch oven instead of the shallow sloped sauté pan I used to recommend, mainly because it contains the splatter [8].

questions.question: Which non-stick pan should I buy?

hybrid.answer:
I'd buy the Our Place Titanium Pro. It's the pan I use for virtually all my non-wok cooking these days [1]. I co-developed it with Our Place, so it's essentially my pan, and you should weigh my pick with that in mind [2].

- **Why the Titanium Pro:** It isn't as non-stick as Teflon, but it's better in most other respects [3]. It sears nicely and evenly, it sears faster, and I can use metal utensils in it [4].
- **When Teflon makes sense:** I mostly avoid coated non-stick now, except for a few specific jobs, and I still use it for an omelet [5]. Teflon coatings have a very limited lifespan and a relatively low temperature range [6]. I wouldn't use it for searing [7].
- **When cast iron is better:** If you want the best possible sear and don't mind a little more time and work, cast iron is the one. It needs a proper preheat of around 10 minutes [7].

The right pan depends on how you cook [8].

questions.question: Is jarred pre-chopped garlic any good?

hybrid.answer:
No, I'd stay away from jarred pre-chopped garlic, whether it's packed in water or in olive oil, because there's hardly any flavor left in it [1]. Fresh garlic that you peel yourself is what I recommend [2].

**Why:** Once garlic is cut, its flavor starts to change and you can't change it back, so any pre-cut garlic tastes different from natural garlic flavor [3]. In my blind tasting, a couple of the samples had a strong citric acid flavor. Citric acid is a preservative that controls water activity and texture, but it completely changes the flavor [4]. I wouldn't use those in any raw setting [4].

**If you cook with it:** Any of them will sort of work for cooking, because cooking tames the sharper pungent flavors and some of the differences even out [5]. Even before cooking, though, there was little aroma in these [6].

**Better shortcuts:** Pre-peeled cloves are fine for most things, especially if you're cooking them [2]. After that, garlic paste may be an acceptable substitute [1].

I'd happily recommend either one; they perform comparably, and the choice comes down to details [1]. If you want to bake bigger pies, go for the Koda 16, which fits up to a 16-inch pizza, more like a New York style, while the Roccbox tops out at 12 inches [2]. If you want fuel flexibility, go for the Roccbox, because you can swap the gas for a wood burner [1].

**Where they differ**
- **Size:** The Koda 16 has a wraparound fire bar that I find great for larger pizzas, since it speeds things up and cooks more evenly [3]. The Roccbox has a single gas jet in the back, but it still gets ripping hot [2].
- **Fuel:** The wood option on the Roccbox adds little flavor to a pizza in the time it bakes, but it's nice for roasting meats or vegetables [3].
- **Exterior heat:** The Roccbox stays nicely cool to the touch on top. The Koda isn't quite as cool, but it's still pretty cool [4].
- **Results:** In a side-by-side bake, both pizzas looked great, though I thought the Roccbox underbelly looked a little better [5]. The Koda cooked a bit faster, which is fine [5].
- **Other cooking:** Both can handle steaks and vegetables. The Koda is big enough for a spatchcock chicken or a loaf of bread [6].

questions.question: Do you ever inject your turkey? And if so, any recommendations on what to use?

hybrid.answer:
I rarely inject my turkey. I've done it in the past, but it's not something I typically do [1]. When you inject, the liquid doesn't get inside the muscle fibers. It sloshes around and separates some of them, so the turkey comes out moist the way a sponge is wet, not the way a juicy piece of meat is [1].

I have enjoyed turkeys that were injected, though, and if you do inject, here's what I'd use:

- **Well-seasoned stock:** Something with salt in it essentially brines the turkey from the inside as well as the outside, which helps it retain more moisture when cooked and sliced [2].
- **Stock and brown butter:** I've done injections with a mixture of turkey stock and brown butter, and I think that can be delicious [2][3].
- **Herb-infused stock or herb butter:** Simmer turkey stock with a lot of herbs, or melt an herb butter, combine it with the turkey stock and inject that [3].

questions.question: Why do you wash meat before stir-frying?

hybrid.answer:
I wash sliced beef in cold water before marinating because it makes the meat noticeably more tender and lets the marinade work better. It's a step I never used to do until I tested it, and side by side it makes a huge difference [1].

- **Better marinade penetration:** Squeezing and massaging the meat in the water pushes out some of the excess juices, which leaves more room for the marinade to get in, so you get more flavor [2].
- **More tender texture:** Washing also loosens up the texture of the muscle, so the beef comes out more tender [2].
- **Possible role of hard water:** An Australian chef I exchanged emails with suggested that, especially where the water is hard, the slightly alkaline makeup of the water may also affect the beef [2].

After washing, I squeeze the meat out in a fine mesh strainer so the excess water doesn't water down the marinade [3]. I also note that adding the washing step would improve the beef in my older beef and broccoli video [4].

questions.question: Just wondering, what is the best way to clean the wok after each use? And should I use the heat & coat in oil technique after each use as well?

hybrid.answer:
Rinse it out right after cooking, using soap if you need it, then put it back on the burner until it's completely dry [1]. I do the reheating to get the wok dry, not for seasoning [1]. A bamboo brush is the best tool for scrubbing [2]. A regular scrubber also works [3].

**Burnt-on food:** Heat the wok to burn it off, then scrub it with water [2]. That won't damage it, and you don't need to worry about scrubbing anything out of a wok [2][4].

**Oil after every use:** Not necessarily. The thin coat of oil matters if you'll store the wok somewhere with moisture in the air, because bare carbon steel can rust [5]. It isn't that important if you use the wok every day or several times a day [5]. With a raw carbon steel wok, don't skip it if you're storing it [5]. It's much less of an issue with a super nitrided wok, since it isn't reactive the way carbon steel is [5].

When you do oil it, use only a very thin layer and wipe it out as if you'd put it in by accident, so it doesn't turn gummy and sticky [6]. Heating the wok first thins the oil, which makes it easier to rub in and out [6].

With the super nitride coating, you don't need to be as careful about drying as with cast iron, but drying still helps maintain the seasoning [7].

questions.question: A genuine question: if a wok doesn't build up layers of polymers like a cast iron, what does it mean for a wok to build up seasoning?

hybrid.answer:
For a wok, seasoning mostly means the initial conversion of raw carbon steel into black oxide, not building layers of polymer [1]. Raw carbon steel is a dull silvery colour. When you heat it on all surfaces, it turns black or bluish black, and that is the initial seasoning step [2]. I'd consider that black oxide layer seasoning, but not a thick polymer layer, which you shouldn't expect or aim for in a wok [3].

**Why polymers don't build up in a wok:**
- The bottom gets very hot and the sides stay cooler, so the metal expands unevenly and any hard polymer layer has a tough time sticking [1].
- Almost every time you cook, you deglaze with liquid like soy sauce or wine, which is often acidic and strips the seasoning [4].

**What happens after that:** seasoning a wok is more of a per-use thing [5]. I wash my wok until it's smooth each time I cook, and I don't build up thick polymer layers over time [6]. After cooking I rinse it, dry it on the burner, and wipe in a very thin coat of oil [7].

**Nitrided woks:** with my super nitrided wok there's no coating when it comes out of the box. You just rinse it and it's ready to cook [8].

questions.question: Is there any advantage to salting hours ahead of time with this technique, or does the long time the steak spends hanging out in the oven make that moot? [reverse sear]

hybrid.answer:
Yes, a little, but only for the sear. For a reverse-sear steak I only need about 45 minutes of salting, and going longer is optional. I haven't said whether the time in the low oven changes the benefit of salting hours ahead.

- **What 45 minutes gets you:** Salt first draws out moisture, then the brine breaks down some muscle proteins and the steak reabsorbs the moisture. Those proteins tighten less when cooked, so less moisture gets squeezed out. You get a juicier steak and more penetrative seasoning [1]. I call 45 minutes about the minimum time for that to happen, and it's enough [1].
- **What going longer adds:** If you leave it uncovered in the fridge overnight, the surface dries out and forms a pellicle, so it sears even better [1]. That is the main extra benefit of salting well ahead.
- **A related test:** In a side-by-side with pan-seared tenderloin, the steak salted overnight and left uncovered got a better brown crust and stayed juicier than the unsalted one [2][3]. I did that test with a pan-seared steak, not a reverse sear.

questions.question: So, Kenji, since you left Cook's Illustrated, they've started to advocate cold searing (starting in a cold pan and flipping every 2 minutes until done). What are your thoughts?

hybrid.answer: I haven't covered cold searing, or the start-in-a-cold-pan, flip-every-couple-of-minutes method, in my videos yet, so I can't give you a verdict on it. The closest thing I've said is about my own preferred method: the reverse sear is still my favorite way to cook a big steak [1]. It starts the steak in a low oven and finishes with a sear, which gives much more even doneness from edge to center than the traditional sear-first method, which leaves a bullseye pattern [2].
